blocks.en: ReLEAF started with one question from the farmers in Ghana: are abiotic stresses really affecting our crops? This question guided our journey from February to October, shaping the development of our project as we investigated farmers’ challenges, consulted experts, and refined our approach to addressing crop stress.

blocks.en: In our project ReLEAF, Human Practices acts as the heart of the team, connecting the research and work we have done in the lab with the real-world needs that help to shape our project. Rather than developing ReLEAF based only on what is scientifically possible, Human Practices allows us to consider how our project could fit into the agricultural world and how it may affect the people who would be interacting with it.

blocks.en: Sitting at the center of various topics such as synthetic biology, climate change, agriculture, and biotechnology, ReLEAF has reached out to a plethora of different stakeholders, including farmers, researchers, professors, agricultural organizations, companies, and members of the public. We deeply value every interaction, hoping to truly be able to gain and understand the different perspectives of differing groups of people, and to identify gaps, challenge our assumptions, and improve our project.

Expert Engagement documents our conversations and collaborations with experts from different fields, organized into individual pipelines based on their areas of expertise and the topics we discussed, as well as our continuous engagement. Farmer Engagement focuses on our conversations with farmers, the primary beneficiaries of our project, and the insights we gained from understanding their experiences and needs. Finally, Public Engagement presents our efforts to communicate with and learn from the wider public. Together, these sections trace how our interactions with different stakeholders continuously shaped and refined ReLEAF.

blocks.en: Throughout the meeting with Prof. Cheng, we introduced our proposed engineered Bacillus subtilis system for detecting plant and environmental stress and responding by producing protective compounds such as trehalose or ACC deaminase. blocks.en: Impact and adaptation
blocks.text: Impact and adaptation

blocks.en: Her feedback made us realize that experimental procedures themselves can interfere with plant stress responses. More importantly, the feedback led us to a shift toward more realistic and controllable plant-growth conditions. She suggested that the project should prioritize agar plate growth for early-stage control, followed by careful transfer to soil. We should carefully manage environmental transitions and stress timing, and use visual ROS staining to improve stress assessment. We also decided to remove osmotic stress from our targeted stresses. Additionally, Prof. Cheng kindly provided us with Arabidopsis seeds and shared valuable guidance on their cultivation and optimal growing conditions.

blocks.en: Event summary

blocks.en: We consulted with Prof. Huang to evaluate the timing, dosage, sensing strategy, and application of our protectant-delivery system. During the discussion, he highlighted that biostimulants can be most effective when applied during the seedling stage to have effects that last longer, which also helps adjust gene regulation signals as cells replicate for long-term protection. Prof. Huang also mentioned that excessive stress or protectant concentrations may affect plant health negatively, so it is important to set appropriate thresholds and validate dosages. From an agricultural angle, hydroponic systems may not completely simulate field conditions, and farmers often prioritize simple application. Therefore, our system should integrate functions such as environmental sensing and weather forecasting to predict stress while keeping it easy for farmers to operate. Prof. Huang also kindly provided us with the B. subtilis WB800 strain, which we further used in other experiments.

blocks.en: These expert consultations helped us shift our Protectant Design pipeline from basic compound testing to a realistic strategy for protecting crops. From an agricultural angle, hydroponic systems may not completely simulate field conditions, and farmers often prioritize simple application. Therefore, our system should integrate functions such as environmental sensing and weather forecasting to predict stress while keeping it easy for farmers to operate. Prof. Huang also kindly provided us with the B. subtilis WB800 strain, which we further used in other experiments.

blocks.en: During our meeting with Mr. Lu, we discussed his company’s business method and his bioreactor, along with asking him questions about the current market of farmers and how he thinks our bioreactor and AIoT can further improve. He advised us to also add a sensor and EC (electrical conductivity sensor) for salinity, along with training our prediction model off of the historical data of the area and to continuously collect data. On the business side, he mentioned that since our bioreactor doesn’t connect to a farm’s irrigation system, it means that farmers have to go there and collect it themselves or use a drone. Mr. Lu also mentioned that we need a more specific adoption plan for farmers, along with the fact that products often pass and become popular by word of mouth, both between farmers and from Ag. blocks.en: Event summary

blocks.en: In the BIO Asia-Taiwan Exhibition, we engaged with different companies, experts, and researchers, gaining many insights from different aspects. One of our most valuable takeaways is that plant stress tolerance depends not only on the presence of protective molecules, such as proline, but also on the processes that regulate their production and use. We also learned that dissolved oxygen monitoring and active aeration/stirring are essential for B. subtilis survival and protein/protectant output, not just passive containment.

blocks.en: Natural farming farmers’ approach focuses on understanding why problems arise and addressing their underlying causes to restore ecological balance without human interference and support. While natural farming often advocates minimal interference, we recognized that zero intervention in crop protection poses a significant risk: the rate of crop loss due to climate stress often outpaces the natural speed at which plants adapt, escalating the threat of severe food crises. This insight reinforced our goal to provide a balanced solution that supports plant resilience without disrupting nature. In response to this, we develop our mathematical model (M1), which aims to represent the conditions of field crops as stress indices and release the appropriate amount of protectant at the right moment. In this way, our model reflects Dr. Li’s idea that technology should address the underlying problem rather than relieve symptoms completely.

blocks.en: From an industry angle, the expert from CH Biotech shared that agricultural waste, such as feathers, can be used to produce signal peptides as biostimulants, which can help crops maintain energy metabolism under stresses, including typhoons and high temperatures, without increasing fertilizer or pesticide use. blocks.en: In our data physicalization station, we wanted a way to turn abstract data on screens and paper into an experience that allowed people to understand the data through interactive maps and activities. blocks.en: Through continuous engagement and discussions with stakeholders from farmers to agricultural organizations and companies to professors and experts, ReLEAF was able to grow into a project grounded in practical application, safety, and community trust. These dialogues ensured that our solution addresses actual field challenges that exist in the real-field. blocks.en: Throughout our project, the question of how we could design a solution that was safe and helpful remained in our minds. To achieve this, we engaged in interviews and meetings with several stakeholders, including farmers, biosafety experts, and plant biologists, which helped ensure that ReLEAF was designed with safety, ethics, and environmental considerations at its core.

To achieve this, we engaged in interviews and meetings with several stakeholders, including farmers, biosafety experts, and plant biologists, which helped ensure that ReLEAF was designed with safety, ethics, and environmental considerations at its core.

blocks.en: First, we were challenged on whether external intervention could undermine plants’ natural resilience. Both Ms. Chen Hui-Wen and Dr. Li Hsu-Ying questioned whether providing external support might only address the symptoms without addressing the underlying causes, which might potentially make crops dependent on technological intervention. The farmers’ feedback helped us understand that success is not just simply about maximizing plant growth, but also providing appropriate support when crops need it.

This then inspired us to incorporate physical damage and extreme weather into our threat analysis and made the decision to move the bioreactor indoors.

Many of the farmers we interviewed were organic or friendly farming practices farmers. However, as ReLEAF uses genetically modified microorganisms, it may not comply with Taiwan’s organic production regulations. This exposed a gap between our original vision of helping farmers and the potential stakeholders that could adopt our system. It showed us that a technical solution is not automatically an appropriate one for every region.

blocks.en: For example, meeting up with Ms. Chen Hui-Wen opened our perspective to the world of natural farming. During this meeting, we learned about the importance of precise stress prediction and targeted application to prevent the overuse of protectants, which can inadvertently reduce crop resilience. While natural farming often advocates minimal interference, we recognized that zero intervention in crop protection poses a significant risk: the rate of crop loss due to climate stress often outpaces the natural speed at which plants adapt, escalating the threat of severe food crises. This insight reinforced our goal to provide a balanced solution that supports plant resilience without disrupting nature.

blocks.en: To ensure our Human Practices framework is completely reproducible, we have structured and open-sourced three complete, downloadable resource packages so future teams can easily adapt and extend our work. First, a clear survey structure, separated into three main domains: Knowledge, Attitude, and Practice (KAP) that efficiently captures the effects and results of our events across farmers, domain experts, and the general public; second, standardized interview question sets categorized across plant biology, protectant design, hardware engineering, and deployment domains to streamline qualitative stakeholder research; and third, our “農友助手” (Farmer’s Assistant) LINE platform, which provides an automatic bot reply that other teams can also use in the future.
